hints: Grab a ruler and measure the black line from X to Y on the photo in millimetres. That is your image size.
Remember magnification = image size divided by real size, so first convert your mm measurement and the real 25 µm into the same units (µm works best here).
walkthrough:
**Measure the image size**

Take a ruler and measure straight from X to Y on the photomicrograph. You should get about 50 mm.

This is how big the cell *looks* on paper, not how big it really is.

**Put both sizes in the same units**

The real cell width is given as $25 \mu m$. We need the image size in µm too.

Remember:
$$1 \text{ mm} = 1000 \text{ } \mu m$$
So:
$$50 \text{ mm} \times 1000 = 50,000 \text{ } \mu m$$

**Apply the magnification formula**

Magnification tells us how many times bigger the image is than real life:
$$\text{magnification} = \frac{\text{image size}}{\text{actual size}}$$
$$\text{magnification} = \frac{50,000}{25} = 2000$$
In standard form this is $2.0 \times 10^3$, which is option C. Well done, that unit conversion is the key trick.

options.A: Too small by 100 times. This would come from a unit conversion error, giving an image size of only 0.5 mm instead of 50 mm.
options.B: Too small by 10 times. This often happens if you forget that 1 mm = 1000 µm and use 100 instead.
options.C: Correct. A 50 mm image divided by a 25 µm real size gives 50,000 / 25 = 2000, or 2.0 x 10^3.
options.D: Too large by 10 times. This would need an image size of 500 mm, which is much bigger than the X to Y line shown.
